question.text:
Given a database relation schema $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{A} 1, \mathrm{~A} 2, \ldots, \mathrm{A}n)$ and a set of functional dependencies $\text{F}$ which hold true on $\mathrm{R}$. Consider the following algorithm :

$\text{Step 1}:$
Construct a list $\mathrm{L}$ consisting of all non-empty subsets of $\{\mathrm{A} 1, \ldots, \text{A}n \}$ (there are $2^n-1$ of them). These subsets are arranged in $\text{L}$ in ascending order of the size of the subset: We get $\mathrm{L}=\langle\mathrm{Z} 1, \mathrm{Z} 2, \ldots, \mathrm{Z}m\rangle$, where $\mathrm{m}$ $=2^n-1$, such that $|Z i| \leq|Z(i+1)|$.
Here $|\mathrm{Zi}|$ denotes the number of elements in the set $\mathrm{Zi}$.

$\text{Step 2}:$
Initialize the set $\text{K}=\{\}$.
While $\text{L}$ is not empty:
remove the first element $\mathrm{Zi}$ from $\mathrm{L}$, and compute $\mathrm{Zi}^{+}$. (Where $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ denotes closure of $\mathrm{X})$
If $\mathrm{Zi}^{+}=\mathrm{R}$, then

  1. Add $\text{Z}i$ to $\mathrm{K}$
  2. Remove any element $\mathrm{Zj}$ from $\mathrm{L}$ if $\mathrm{Zi} \subset \mathrm{Zj}$.

$\text{Step 3}:$
Output $\text{K}$ as the final result.

What is $\mathrm{K}?$

  1. Set of all super keys
  2. Set of all candidate keys
  3. Set of all non-candidate keys
  4. Set of all super keys which are not candidate keys

$\mathrm{B}^+$-trees have different structures for leaf and non-leaf nodes.
In $\mathrm{B}^+$- tree leaf node contains keys and record pointer associated with it and a block pointer pointing to the next leaf node. Non-leaf nodes contains only keys and child pointer, there is no need to store record pointer at non-leaf node, because all keys are ultimately present on leaf node. For leaf node order will be maximum number of keys, record pointer pair a node can hold, but order of non leaf node is determined by maximum child pointers it can have.

$\mathrm{A}\; \mathrm{B}^{+}-$tree index is to be built on the Name attribute of the relation STUDENT. Assume that all student names are of length 8 bytes, disk blocks are of size 512 bytes, and index pointers, record pointers are of size $4$ bytes, $5$ bytes respectively. Given this scenario, the best choice for the order of leaf node and non-leaf node is $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$ respectively. Then what is $\mathrm{Y}-\mathrm{X}$ ?

Codd's rule of physical data independence is that

  1. all information in the database is to be represented in one and only one way, namely by values in column positions within rows of tables.
  2. all views that are theoretically updatable must be updatable by the system.
  3. changes that are made to the physical storage representations or access methods must not require changes be made to application programs.
  4. changes that are made to tables that do not modify any of the data already stored in the tables must not require changes be made to application programs.

A $\text{B}^+$ Tree of order $\text{M}$ has the following properties:

  1. The root is either a leaf or has between $2$ and $\text{M}$ children.
  2. All non-leaf nodes (except the root) have between $\lceil \text{M} / 2\rceil$ and $\text{M}$ children.
  3. All leaves are at the same depth.

All data records are stored at the leaves.

Internal nodes have "keys" guiding to the leaves.

Leaves store between $\lceil \text{L} / 2\rceil$ and $\text{L}$ data records, where $\text{L}$ can be equal to $\text{M}$ or can be different.

The number of levels in the tree is also called the height i.e. a $\text{B}^+$ tree with a single node has height $1.$

Two more exotic relational algebra operators are the semijoin $(\ltimes)$ and antijoin $(\triangleright)$. Semijoin is the same as natural join, except only attributes of the first relation are returned in the result. For example, if we have relations $\textsf{Student(ID, name)}$ and $\textsf{Enrolled(ID, course)},$ and not all students are enrolled in courses, then the query "Student $\ltimes$ Enrolled" returns the ID and name of all students who are enrolled in at least one course. In the general case, $\text{E}_1 \ltimes \text{E}_2$ returns all tuples in the result of expression $\text{E}_1$ such that there is at least one tuple in the result of $\mathrm{E}_2$ with matching values for the shared attributes. antijoin is the converse: $\text{E}_1 \triangleright \text{E}_2$ returns all tuples in the result of expression $\text{E}_1$ such that there are no tuples in the result of $\text{E}_2$ with matching values for the shared attributes. For example, the query "Student $\triangleright$ Enrolled" returns the ID and name of all students who are not enrolled in any courses.

  3. $(\mathrm{E}_1 \triangleright \mathrm{E}_2) \cup(\mathrm{E}_1 \ltimes \mathrm{E}_2)=\mathrm{E}_1$

  4. $(\mathrm{E}_1 \triangleright \mathrm{E}_2) \bowtie(\mathrm{E}_1 \ltimes \mathrm{E}_2)=\mathrm{E}_1$
